newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE - Egypt wants out of world wheat spotlight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Egypt wants out of world wheat spotlight.

text.p: Egypt wants to withdraw from its key position in global grain markets by the next century, when it hopes to harvest the gains of an ambitious and controversial scheme to cultivate almost all the wheat it needs.

Agriculture Minister Youssef Wali said in remarks published last week that Egypt, a major purchaser whose import decisions have swayed international markets for years, aims to grow at least 75 percent of its consumption needs by the year 2000.

"It'll take us time to replace the six to 6.5 million tonnes (which Egypt imports each year), probably four or five years or even more, but it most certainly is feasible," said Alaa el-Khouly, a consultant at the Ministry of Supply for the import substitution project.
"There are plenty of areas to cultivate, the productivity per feddan (acre) is increasing and we're also planning to decrease wheat consumption by using other crops," he added.
Egyptians consume about 11 million tonnes of wheat annually and with a population growth rate of about two percent a year, consumption is set to rise further.
The agriculture and supply ministries say they have been working on strategies to boost production and reduce consumption since the beginning of the 1980s.

But this year, the government has taken the idea seriously, especially since President Hosni Mubarak launched a grand project to develop a New Valley in the south and relocate farm lands from their ancient site in the Nile delta.
Egypt has increased its acreage of wheat and planted high-yielding varieties. Officials say they expect a harvest of 5.9 million tonnes in 1997. In the 1996 season, Egypt grew 5.7 million tonnes.
Grain market analysts and traders take a sceptical view of the government's optimistic predictions.

"It's very noble of them and I think they will achieve quite a bit more, but by and large Egypt is an irrigated country and it doesn't have the comparative advantage other countries do," said an official who sells Egypt millions of tonnes of grain a year.

"Egypt can produce any crop it chooses...I don't understand why Egypt is so bothered by this. It's this strong sense of nationalism, that Pharaonic Egypt was a major breadbasket. It's definitely a political decision," he told Reuters.
EGYPT SEEKS SELF-SUFFICIENCY IN WHEAT BY 2002

Mohammed el-Sayed, an agricultural economist at the ministry, wistfully refers to the days when Egypt exported wheat to Saudi Arabia early this century and forecasts that the country can be self-sufficient by 2002.

"The gap between consumption and production is getting smaller and the agriculture ministry is working hard to make it disappear. It's ludicrous to suggest that Egypt should remain dependent on imports given price fluctuations," Sayed said.
A plethora of cash crops compete for the cultivated land in Egypt which makes up about three percent of the country's total area of approximately 400,000 square miles (1.04 milion square km).

Most of that land lies in the Nile delta. Although land reclamation schemes have increased the amount, traders say it does not make economic sense to try to grow a crop which is ill-suited to the climate and the region.

"It just doesn't pay to plant the darn stuff. It's cheaper to import because there will always be cheaper producers like the United States," said Wayne Bacon, vice president of traders Oriac International.

Nationalisation of land in the 1950s and its sale in small quantities to labourers has made Egypt's wheat farms patchy at best, particularly compared with the rain-fed wheat plains of Kansas or Australia.
GOVERNMENT PINS HOPES ON CULTIVATING RAIN-FED AREAS

The government is pinning its hopes on cultivating rain-fed areas in the Sinai and on the north coast as well as using the vast landscape of the New Valley. It is also encouraging farmers to plant the cash crop and has offered to buy the grain for about $30 a tonne, which is higher than market prices.
Sayed said that Egypt is boosting its production of crops like rice and corn which he says can be easily substituted for wheat. Rice exports can also be used to fund some wheat imports, he added.
Both the government and traders agree that only time will tell if the self-sufficiency scheme will succeed or fail.

Mubarak has said that developing the New Valley project will take decades. It also needs vast amounts of capital. But a lack of pioneering spirit needed to open new frontiers hinders the creation of new farms, while age-old land rights prevent the amalgamation of existing acreage.

"I'm not as optimistic as the government but only time will tell. It's a goal which will take a lot of work, and the cost of imports is less than the cost of all that they are doing, but then again they're thinking long-term," another trader said.
